knowledgeBase.summary: Practical Linux system administration reference covering file systems, permissions, process management, networking, systemd, package management, log analysis, SSH, cron, and performance monitoring — built for daily IT troubleshooting.

sections.title: File System
sections.content:
Linux uses a single-rooted hierarchical file system starting at /. Key directories: /etc (system config), /var (variable data, logs), /home (user directories), /usr (user programs), /tmp (temporary files, often cleared on reboot), /proc and /sys (virtual filesystems exposing kernel/process info).

Navigation and inspection:
pwd                     # print working directory
ls -la                  # list all files, long format, including hidden
df -h                   # disk free space, human-readable
du -sh /path/*          # disk usage per item in a directory
lsblk                   # list block devices and mount points
mount | column -t       # show mounted filesystems
findmnt /var            # show mount info for a specific path

Finding files:
find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1     # log files modified in the last day
find / -size +100M 2>/dev/null            # files larger than 100MB, suppress permission errors
locate filename                            # fast search using the locate database

Symbolic vs hard links: ln -s target linkname creates a symlink (pointer, can cross filesystems); ln target linkname creates a hard link (same inode, must be same filesystem).

sections.title: User & Permission Management
sections.content:
Linux permissions use three classes (owner, group, other) and three permission types (read, write, execute), represented as rwxrwxrwx or octal (e.g. 755).

Viewing and changing permissions:
ls -l file.txt                  # view permissions
chmod 755 script.sh             # rwxr-xr-x
chmod u+x script.sh             # add execute for owner only
chown user:group file.txt       # change owner and group
chown -R user:group /path/      # recursive

User management:
useradd -m -s /bin/bash newuser    # create user with home dir and bash shell
usermod -aG sudo username          # add user to sudo group (Debian/Ubuntu)
usermod -aG wheel username         # add user to wheel group (RHEL/CentOS)
passwd username                    # set/change password
userdel -r username                # delete user and home directory
id username                        # show UID, GID, and group memberships
groups username                    # list groups a user belongs to

Sudo configuration: edit with visudo (never edit /etc/sudoers directly). Common entry: username ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL grants passwordless sudo.

Special permission bits: setuid (chmod u+s), setgid (chmod g+s), sticky bit (chmod +t, commonly on /tmp to prevent users deleting others' files).

sections.title: Process Management
sections.content:
Every running program is a process with a PID. Processes have a state (running, sleeping, zombie, stopped) and a parent-child relationship tree.

Viewing processes:
ps aux                          # all processes, BSD-style full listing
ps -ef                          # all processes, standard format with PPID
top                              # live updating process viewer
htop                             # improved interactive version
pstree                           # show process tree
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10   # top 10 CPU-consuming processes
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -10   # top 10 memory-consuming processes

Controlling processes:
kill -15 PID          # graceful termination (SIGTERM)
kill -9 PID            # force kill (SIGKILL) — last resort
killall processname    # kill all processes matching a name
pkill -f "pattern"      # kill by matching command line pattern
nice -n 10 command      # start a process with lower priority
renice -n 5 -p PID      # change priority of a running process

Background/foreground job control:
command &              # run in background
jobs                   # list background jobs
fg %1                  # bring job 1 to foreground
bg %1                  # resume job 1 in background
nohup command &         # run immune to hangup signal
disown                 # detach a job from the current shell

A zombie process (state Z in ps) means the child finished but the parent hasn't reaped it.

sections.title: Networking on Linux
sections.content:
Modern Linux networking tools center on the ip command (replacing the older ifconfig/route/netstat).

Interface and address info:
ip a                      # show all interfaces and addresses
ip link show               # show interface status (up/down)
ip route                   # show routing table
ip route get 8.8.8.8       # show which route would be used to reach an IP

Connections and listening ports:
ss -tulpn                  # TCP/UDP listening sockets with process names
ss -tan state established  # established TCP connections
lsof -i :8080               # what process is using port 8080
fuser -k 8080/tcp            # kill whatever is using port 8080

DNS:
dig example.com              # detailed DNS query
dig +short example.com        # just the IP
nslookup example.com
resolvectl status              # systemd-resolved status
cat /etc/resolv.conf            # configured DNS servers

Connectivity testing:
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8                  # 4 pings
traceroute example.com               # path to destination
mtr example.com                       # combines ping+traceroute, live updating
curl -v https://example.com            # verbose HTTP request
nc -zv host 22                          # test if a TCP port is open

Interface configuration (temporary, lost on reboot unless persisted):
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip link set eth0 up

sections.title: systemd & Services
sections.content:
systemd is the init system and service manager on most modern Linux distributions.

Managing services:
systemctl status nginx              # check status
systemctl start nginx               # start now
systemctl stop nginx                # stop now
systemctl restart nginx             # stop then start
systemctl reload nginx              # reload config without full restart
systemctl enable nginx              # start automatically on boot
systemctl disable nginx             # don't start on boot
systemctl is-active nginx           # quick active/inactive check
systemctl is-enabled nginx          # quick boot-enabled check

Finding problems:
systemctl list-units --failed       # show all failed services
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
journalctl -u nginx -f                # live tail logs for a service
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -xe                        # recent logs with explanations
journalctl -b                         # logs since last boot
journalctl -p err                     # only error-level and above

Custom service units live in /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service. After editing:
systemctl daemon-reload    # required after editing any unit file
systemctl restart myapp

Minimal unit file:
[Unit]
Description=My App
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/myapp/run.py
Restart=on-failure
User=appuser

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sections.title: Package Management
sections.content:
Debian/Ubuntu uses APT, RHEL/CentOS/Fedora uses DNF/YUM.

APT (Debian/Ubuntu):
sudo apt update                   # refresh package index
sudo apt upgrade                  # upgrade all installed packages
sudo apt install nginx            # install a package
sudo apt remove nginx             # remove, keep config files
sudo apt purge nginx              # remove including config files
sudo apt autoremove               # remove unused dependencies
apt list --installed | grep nginx  # check if installed
apt show nginx                     # package details
dpkg -L nginx                      # list files installed by a package

DNF (RHEL/CentOS 8+/Fedora):
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf upgrade
sudo dnf install nginx
sudo dnf remove nginx
dnf list installed | grep nginx
rpm -ql nginx                      # list files installed by a package

Finding what package provides a file:
dpkg -S /usr/bin/nginx              # Debian/Ubuntu
rpm -qf /usr/bin/nginx               # RHEL/CentOS

Holding a package at its current version:
sudo apt-mark hold nginx            # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf versionlock nginx          # RHEL/CentOS

sections.title: Log Analysis
sections.content:
Key log locations: /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages (general system log), /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure (authentication events), /var/log/kern.log (kernel messages), /var/log/dmesg (boot-time kernel ring buffer), application-specific logs under /var/log/<appname>/.

Reading and filtering:
tail -f /var/log/syslog              # live follow
tail -n 100 /var/log/syslog           # last 100 lines
less /var/log/syslog                   # paginated view, /search inside
grep "error" /var/log/syslog            # filter for a string
grep -i "failed" /var/log/auth.log | tail -20
zgrep "error" /var/log/syslog.1.gz       # search inside gzipped rotated logs

Combining with awk/sed for structured extraction:
awk '{print $1, $2, $5}' /var/log/syslog        # extract specific columns
sed -n '100,200p' /var/log/syslog                 # print lines 100-200

Log rotation is managed by logrotate, configured in /etc/logrotate.d/.
cat /var/lib/logrotate/status
logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf    # dry run

For systemd-based logging, journalctl largely supersedes flat log files for service-level logs.

sections.title: SSH
sections.content:
SSH is the standard for remote Linux administration.

Basic connection:
ssh user@host                       # connect
ssh -p 2222 user@host                # custom port
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mykey user@host         # specific private key
ssh -v user@host                      # verbose, useful for debugging

Key-based authentication:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "comment"     # generate a modern key pair
ssh-copy-id user@host                   # copy public key to remote authorized_keys

SSH config file (~/.ssh/config) for shortcuts:
Host myserver
    HostName 192.168.1.50
    User admin
    Port 2222
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/mykey
Then just: ssh myserver

File transfer:
scp file.txt user@host:/path/             # copy local to remote
scp user@host:/path/file.txt .             # copy remote to local
scp -r folder/ user@host:/path/             # recursive directory copy
rsync -avz folder/ user@host:/path/           # only copies diffs, better for large transfers

Server-side hardening (/etc/ssh/sshd_config):
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
AllowUsers admin deploy
After editing: sudo systemctl restart sshd. Always test a new connection in a separate terminal before closing your current session.

sections.title: Cron Jobs
sections.content:
Cron schedules recurring tasks. Format: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command.

Editing crontab:
crontab -e          # edit current user's crontab
crontab -l           # list current user's cron jobs
crontab -r           # remove all cron jobs
sudo crontab -e -u username    # edit another user's crontab

Examples:
0 2 * * *        /opt/scripts/backup.sh          # daily at 2:00 AM
*/15 * * * *      /opt/scripts/healthcheck.sh      # every 15 minutes
0 0 * * 0          /opt/scripts/weekly-report.sh     # weekly, Sunday midnight
0 9-17 * * 1-5      /opt/scripts/business-hours.sh      # hourly, business hours weekdays

System-wide cron locations: /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/, /etc/cron.hourly/, /etc/crontab.

Debugging cron jobs (cron has a minimal environment, no full PATH):
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
# Always use absolute paths inside cron scripts
# Redirect output to a log for debugging:
0 2 * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

Check if cron ran: grep CRON /var/log/syslog or journalctl -u cron.

For user-level scheduled tasks without root, systemd timers are a modern alternative to cron with better logging via journalctl.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring
sections.content:
CPU:
top                       # live view, press 1 for per-core breakdown
htop                       # nicer interactive version
mpstat 1 5                  # per-CPU stats, 5 samples 1 second apart
uptime                       # load average (1, 5, 15 min)
nproc                         # number of CPU cores
lscpu                          # detailed CPU info

Memory:
free -h                    # human-readable memory summary
vmstat 1 5                  # virtual memory stats over time
cat /proc/meminfo             # detailed breakdown
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head    # top memory consumers

Disk I/O:
iostat -x 1 5               # extended disk I/O stats
iotop                         # live per-process disk I/O
df -h                          # disk space usage
du -sh /* 2>/dev/null            # size per top-level directory

Network:
iftop                       # live bandwidth per connection
nload                        # simple live bandwidth graph
ss -s                         # socket statistics summary

Load average interpretation: three numbers are 1/5/15-minute averages of the run queue length. On a 4-core system, a load of 4.0 means cores are fully utilized.

Quick health check one-liner:
echo "=== CPU ==="; uptime; echo "=== MEM ==="; free -h; echo "=== DISK ==="; df -h; echo "=== TOP ==="; ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -5

sections.title: Log Management and Log Rotation
sections.content:
Effective log management prevents disk exhaustion and ensures system observability. Linux environments typically utilize two primary systems: `logrotate` for traditional flat-file logs and `systemd-journald` for binary-indexed system logs.

### Logrotate
`logrotate` automates the rotation, compression, and removal of log files. It is typically executed daily via a systemd timer or cron job.

*   **Configuration:**
    *   Global settings: `/etc/logrotate.conf`
    *   Service-specific rules: `/etc/logrotate.d/`
*   **Key Directives:**
    *   `rotate <count>`: Number of rotated files to retain.
    *   `size <size>`: Rotate if the log exceeds this size (e.g., `100M`).
    *   `compress`: Gzip rotated logs.
    *   `copytruncate`: Truncate the original log file in place after creating a copy (essential for services that cannot close/reopen log files).
    *   `postrotate` / `endscript`: Commands to run after rotation (e.g., `systemctl reload nginx`).

**Example Configuration (`/etc/logrotate.d/myapp`):**
```text
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 myapp myapp
    postrotate
        /usr/bin/systemctl reload myapp > /dev/null 2>&1 || true
    endscript
}
```
*   **Validation:** Test configurations without performing rotation using the debug flag:
    `logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/myapp`
*   **Force Rotation:** Manually trigger rotation for testing:
    `logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/myapp`

### Systemd Journal
`journald` captures logs from the kernel, initrd, and services. Logs are stored in a binary format, providing structured, searchable data.

*   **Persistence:** By default, logs may be volatile. To ensure persistence across reboots, ensure the storage directory exists:
    `mkdir -p /var/log/journal`
    Then, set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and restart the service: `systemctl restart systemd-journald`.
*   **Querying (`journalctl`):**
    *   View all logs: `journalctl`
    *   Follow logs in real-time: `journalctl -f`
    *   Filter by service: `journalctl -u <service_name>`
    *   Filter by time: `journalctl --since "1 hour ago"` or `journalctl --until "2026-08-01"`
    *   Filter by priority: `journalctl -p err` (0: emerg, 3: err, 4: warn, 6: info).
*   **Retention:** Manage disk usage by limiting the journal size in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`:
    *   `SystemMaxUse=500M`
    *   `MaxRetentionSec=1month`
    *   Apply changes by restarting the service or using `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` to manually clear old entries.

sections.title: Configuring Log Rotation and Retention
sections.content:
Log rotation is managed via the `logrotate` utility, which automates the archiving, compression, and removal of log files to prevent storage exhaustion.

### Configuration Structure
*   **Global Configuration:** `/etc/logrotate.conf` defines system-wide defaults.
*   **Service-Specific Configuration:** Files located in `/etc/logrotate.d/` override global settings. Always create new files here rather than editing the global configuration to ensure maintainability and package compatibility.

### Syntax and Directives
Configuration files use a block-based syntax. Directives within the braces apply to the specified log path(s).

```text
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 root adm
    copytruncate
}
```

#### Key Directives
*   **Rotation Triggers:**
    *   `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `yearly`: Time-based rotation intervals.
    *   `size <size>`: Rotates when the log exceeds the specified size (e.g., `100M`).
    *   `maxsize <size>`: Forces rotation if the log exceeds the size, regardless of the time interval.
*   **Retention and Management:**
    *   `rotate <count>`: Number of rotated log files to retain before deletion.
    *   `compress`: Gzip-compresses rotated logs.
    *   `delaycompress`: Defers compression of the most recent rotated file until the next cycle (useful if a service keeps the file open).
*   **File Handling:**
    *   `copytruncate`: Copies the log file and then truncates the original to zero size. Essential for services that cannot close their log file handles.
    *   `create <mode> <owner> <group>`: Creates a new, empty log file after rotation with specified permissions.
    *   `missingok`: Prevents errors if the log file is missing.
    *   `notifempty`: Skips rotation if the log file is empty.
*   **Execution Hooks:**
    *   `prerotate` / `postrotate`: Scripts executed before or after the rotation process (must be enclosed in `endscript`).

### Verification and Testing
To validate configuration changes without affecting production logs, use the debug flag. This performs a "dry run" and outputs the actions `logrotate` would take.

*   **Dry Run:**
    `logrotate --debug /etc/logrotate.conf`
*   **Force Rotation:**
    To test a specific configuration file immediately, bypassing time-based triggers:
    `logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/<service_name>`
*   **Verbose Execution:**
    `logrotate -v /etc/logrotate.d/<service_name>`

### Operational Notes
*   **Permissions:** Ensure the user running `logrotate` has write access to the log directory. If the service runs as a non-root user, use the `su <user> <group>` directive within the configuration block to ensure the new log file is created with correct ownership.
*   **Scheduling:** `logrotate` is typically invoked by a systemd timer (`logrotate.timer`) or a cron job (`/etc/cron.daily/logrotate`). If using `hourly` rotation, ensure the system scheduler is configured to trigger the utility at that frequency.

glossary.definition: A data structure storing metadata about a file (permissions, owner, size, location) but not its name — names map to inodes via directory entries.
Process ID — a unique number identifying a running process.
Parent Process ID — the PID of the process that spawned this one.
A process that has finished but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't read its exit status yet.
A background process running without direct user interaction, typically providing a service (e.g. sshd, nginx).
Signal 15 — a graceful termination request a process can catch and handle before exiting.
Signal 9 — an immediate, unblockable termination the OS enforces; the process cannot clean up.
A measure of system demand: the average number of processes waiting for or using the CPU over 1, 5, and 15 minute windows.
A systemd configuration file (.service, .timer, etc) defining how a service or scheduled task runs.
The command-line tool for querying logs collected by systemd's journal service.
A permission bit on a directory preventing users from deleting files they don't own, even with write access to the directory (commonly set on /tmp).
A symbolic link — a special file pointing to another file or directory by path, can cross filesystem boundaries.

commonIssues.cause: Config syntax error, missing dependency, permission issue, or port conflict.
commonIssues.solution: Run systemctl status servicename for the immediate error, then journalctl -u servicename -n 50 for context. Check port conflicts with ss -tulpn | grep PORT. Verify file permissions match the service's running user.

commonIssues.problem: Disk is full and the system is misbehaving
commonIssues.cause: Logs, old kernels, or application data have consumed all available space.
commonIssues.solution: Run df -h to confirm which partition is full, then du -sh /var/log/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head to find large log directories. Truncate or rotate logs with journalctl --vacuum-size=200M. Check for orphaned old kernels with dpkg -l | grep linux-image.

commonIssues.problem: Permission denied when running a script that should be executable
commonIssues.cause: The execute bit isn't set, or the shebang line is missing/wrong.
commonIssues.solution: Run chmod +x script.sh. Verify the first line is a valid shebang like #!/bin/bash. If on a noexec-mounted filesystem, move the script or invoke with bash script.sh.

commonIssues.problem: Network interface is down after a reboot
commonIssues.cause: Network configuration wasn't persisted, or NetworkManager/netplan config is misconfigured.
commonIssues.solution: Check ip a to confirm interface state. On Ubuntu with netplan, check /etc/netplan/*.yaml and run sudo netplan apply. On NetworkManager systems, use nmcli device status and nmcli connection up <name>.

commonIssues.problem: High load average but CPU usage looks low in top
commonIssues.cause: Processes are likely blocked on I/O wait, not CPU-bound.
commonIssues.solution: Check the wa column in top or run vmstat 1 5 — high wa percentage confirms I/O bottleneck. Use iotop to identify the process causing I/O load. Check disk health with smartctl -a /dev/sda if available.

commonIssues.problem: SSH connection refused or times out
commonIssues.cause: SSH daemon isn't running, firewall is blocking the port, or wrong port/IP is used.
commonIssues.solution: On the server: systemctl status sshd to confirm it's running. Check firewall rules with ufw status or iptables -L -n. Confirm SSH is listening with ss -tulpn | grep :22. From the client, verify connectivity with nc -zv host 22 first.

commonIssues.problem: Cron job isn't running even though the schedule looks correct
commonIssues.cause: Cron runs with a minimal environment, so scripts relying on environment variables or relative paths silently fail.
commonIssues.solution: Use absolute paths everywhere. Add an explicit PATH at the top of the crontab. Redirect output to a log file. Verify cron itself ran via grep CRON /var/log/syslog.

commonIssues.problem: Out of memory errors or the OOM killer terminating processes
commonIssues.cause: A process is consuming more memory than available, or swap is exhausted.
commonIssues.solution: Check free -h for memory and swap usage. Identify the culprit with ps aux --sort=-%mem | head. Review dmesg | grep -i "out of memory" or journalctl -k | grep -i oom to confirm and identify the killed process.

commonIssues.problem: Package installation fails with dependency conflicts
commonIssues.cause: Repository metadata is stale, or there's a version conflict.
commonIssues.solution: Run apt update (or dnf check-update) first. For stuck dependencies, try apt --fix-broken install. Check apt-cache policy packagename for available versions and pin manually if needed.

commonIssues.problem: User can't sudo even though they're in the sudo group
commonIssues.cause: Group membership requires a new login session, or the group name differs by distro.
commonIssues.solution: Have the user log out and back in (or run newgrp sudo). Confirm with groups username. Verify the correct group name: Debian/Ubuntu use sudo, RHEL/CentOS use wheel.
